generatedProse.concept-context: Across disciplines, Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle is used to turn experience into learning, because so much of any field is learned by doing. The cycle insists you move past what happened and how it felt to abstract conceptualisation, connecting the experience to ideas, evidence or established practice, before planning what to change. That conceptualisation stage is where an anecdote about a project or a task becomes genuine learning.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students reflecting on the same group project that went wrong when a deadline was missed.

Student A stops after the first two stages of the cycle. Student A describes the missed deadline and the tension it caused, then observes feeling frustrated and that the group communicated poorly. The account is accurate, but it ends at observation. No concept is brought in to explain it, and no plan follows. It is a description with feelings attached.

Student B carries the same experience through all four stages. After describing and observing, Student B reaches abstract conceptualisation, drawing on ideas about shared responsibility to see that no one had owned the deadline because everyone assumed someone else would. Then comes active experimentation: next time, named roles and a shared timeline agreed at the first meeting. That plan starts the next cycle.

Both began from the same project. Only Student B used the whole cycle, turning an event into a concept-led plan rather than a retelling.
generatedProse.summary: Across disciplines, Kolb's cycle turns an experience such as a project or a task into learning by carrying it through concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation and active experimentation. Used critically, it forces the step from describing what happened to explaining it with concepts and planning what to change. You can now structure a reflection with the cycle, tell critical reflection from description, and reach a reasoned plan. The next lesson turns this into writing.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Student B's reflection critical rather than descriptive?

items.text: Student B explained the missed deadline using concepts such as shared responsibility, and reached a concrete plan.
Student B described the missed deadline and the tension in more vivid detail.
Student B spent longer describing how frustrated they felt.
Student B identified which group member was most at fault.

feedback.correct: That's right. Explaining the experience with concepts and reaching a plan is what makes a reflection critical.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the stages of the cycle that Student A left out.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Student B's reflection was critical because it explained the episode with concepts and reached a plan, not because the description was more vivid or the feeling stronger.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
